sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Kyūshū** ​(*kyushu*) — ‌The Nine ‌Provinces — ​belongs ​to the ​Japanese tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ​"South, ‌Volcanoes, Origins". ​The name ‌means ​"'Nine provinces' ‌(九州)"[^1].

Kyūshū ​is Japan's ​front ​door: the ​island facing ​Korea ‌and China ​across the ‌narrowest straits, ​where ‌the continent's ​rice, Buddhism, ‌and ​iron first ‌arrived — ​and where ​the ‌Mongol fleets, ‌the Portuguese ‌traders, ​and the ​Jesuit fathers ‌all made ​their ​landfall. The ‌gateway of ​Japan ​has always ‌stood open ​on this ‌shore, ​even when ​the country ​tried ​to shut ‌it.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name ‌as **Kyūshū** ​and serves ​its ‌temple at ‌[kyūshū.com](https://xn--kysh-w7ac.com). The ‌restoration preserves ‌the ​long ū ‌vowels — ​distinctive ​features the ​ASCII form ‌loses — ​which ​places the ​name in ‌Tier ​1. The ​plain ASCII ​form *kyushu* ‌survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for this ​name; ​**Kyūshū** is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ​of the ‌reconstructed spoken ​form. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"'Nine provinces' ‌(九州)"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form *kyushu* ​survives only ​because ​the early ​domain-name system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ‌is a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode ‌restoration **Kyūshū** ​recovers the ​vowel length ‌of ‌the original ‌directly in ​the address ​bar. ‌The restoration ​preserves the ​long ‌ū vowels ​— distinctive ​features the ‌ASCII ​form loses ‌— which ​places the ​name ​in Tier ​1.

The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

​- **k** ‌→ **K** ​— ​Same letter
‌- **y** ‌→ **y** ‌— ‌Same letter
​- **u** ‌→ ​**ū** — ​Macron marks ​the long ‌vowel
​- **s** ​→ **s** ​— Same ‌letter
​- **h** ​→ **h** ​— ‌Same letter
​- **u** ‌→ **ū** ​— ‌Macron marks ​the long ‌vowel

The ‌project ​holds the ​domain **kyūshū.com** ​(xn--kysh-w7ac.com) ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/kjɯː.ɕɯː/** — ​Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

‌For ​the modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​KYOO-shoo, ‌with ​the ​compressed ky- ​onset ​and ​long ‌vowels.

Kindred ​and ‌historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

‌- ​**Japanese** ‌— 九州
​- ​**Ancient ‌name** ‌— Tsukushi
‌- ​**Owned ​form** ‌— Kyūshū

​Kyūshū ​九州 ‌— ​"Nine Provinces" ​— ‌carries ​the ‌long ū ​in ​both ​syllables, ​both preserved ‌in ‌the ​restoration. ‌The name ​remembers ​the ‌island's ‌ancient division ‌into ‌nine ​provinces; ‌its older ​name, ​Tsukushi, ​appears ‌in the ​earliest ​chronicles ​as ‌the gateway ​of ​the ​gods' ‌descent. Both ​syllables ‌are ​long ‌in kana ​(きゅうしゅう); ‌the ‌two ​macrons of ​the ​restoration ​are ‌the two ‌doubled ​vowels.

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.body:
The ​original ‌script ‌for ​this ​japanese ​name ​has ​not ‌yet ​been ​added to ‌PUNICODEX. ​The ‌form ​shown ‌is ​a ​scholarly ​transliteration.[^1]

​The ​form ‌**Kyūshū** ​is ‌therefore ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌rather ​than ‌an ​attested ​ancient ‌spelling; it ‌encodes ‌the ​reconstructed ​sound ‌of ​the ​name ‌for ​modern ​use, ‌and ​no ‌mark ​in ​it ​is ​decorative.

‌Written ‌九州: ​kyū ‌(nine) ​plus shū ​(province). ‌The ‌island's ‌ancient ‌name ​筑紫 ‌(Tsukushi) ​is ​preserved ​in ‌the ​Kojiki's ​island-birth ​account ‌— ​"Kyūshū" ​is ​the ‌administrative ​name ‌that ​replaced the ‌mythic ​one ‌and ‌quietly ​kept ​the ​older ​island's ‌memory ‌of ​division.

sections.body:
Kyūshū ​is Japan's ‌front ‌door: the ​island facing ​Korea ​and China ​across ​the narrowest ‌straits, where ​the ​continent's rice, ‌Buddhism, ​and iron ‌first arrived ​— ‌and where ​the ​Mongol fleets, ​the Portuguese ​traders, ​and the ‌Jesuit ​fathers all ‌made ​their landfall. ‌The gateway ​of ‌Japan has ​always ‌stood open ​on this ​shore, ‌even when ‌the ‌country tried ​to shut ​it.[^1]

‌### The ​Straits

​Tsushima and ‌Korea are ​a ​day's sail ‌— ​Asia has ‌always ​been closer ​here than ​Tōkyō.

​### The ‌Kamikaze

‌The "divine ​wind" typhoons ‌of ​1274 and ​1281 ‌that shattered ‌two Mongol ‌invasion ‌fleets off ​this ‌coast.

### ​Nagasaki

The ​one ​window kept ‌open ​in the ​closed ​country: two ‌centuries of ​Dutch ​and Chinese ​trade ‌through a ​single fan-shaped ‌island.

​### The ‌Christian ​Century

Xavier's ‌1549 landing, ‌a ​quarter-million converts, ​the ​Shimabara rising, ​and the ‌hidden ‌Christians' 250-year ​secret.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Kyūshū claims ​the mythology of ‌beginnings: the chronicles ‌land the sun ​goddess's grandson on ​its peaks, ​and its storms ​wrote themselves into ​the national soul.[^1]

‌### Ninigi on ​Takachiho (The Descent)

​The Kojiki and ‌Nihon Shoki bring ​the heavenly grandson ‌Ninigi down to ​earth on ‌the peak of ​Takachiho — placed ​by tradition in ​Kyūshū's mountains — ​where he marries ​the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime. ‌She proves her ​divine conception by ‌setting fire ​to the birthing ‌hut and delivering ​three sons amid ‌the flames; their ​line leads to ‌Jimmu, the first ​emperor. The imperial ​charter myth is, ‌geographically, a Kyūshū ‌story.[^2]

### ‌The Divine Wind ​(The Storm)

Twice ​the Mongol-Chinese fleets ‌of Kublai Khan ​reached Kyūshū — ​1274 and 1281, ‌the second numbering ​thousands of ships ​— and twice, ‌after hard ​fighting on the ‌Hakata beaches, typhoons ​destroyed the armadas. ​The shrines had ​prayed for deliverance, ​and the nation ‌named the storm ‌kamikaze, "divine wind": ​weather as providence, ‌and the ​coast of Hakata ​Bay as the ‌sacrificial altar of ‌the world's largest ‌seaborne invasions.

### ‌The Kirishitan Century ​(The Hidden Faith)

‌Francis Xavier landed ​at Kagoshima in ​1549; within ​decades Kyūshū had ‌a quarter-million Christians, ​daimyō baptized with ​their domains, and ​seminaries at Arima ‌and Azuchi. Then ​came the turn: ​persecution, crucifixions at ​Nagasaki, the ‌Shimabara-Amakusa rising of ​1637 — and ‌250 years of ​hidden Christians keeping ‌Latin prayers in ​corrupted Japanese, baptizing ‌in secret, venerating ‌statues of Kannon ​as Maria. Their ​revelation in ​1865, when farmers ​of Urakami knelt ‌before a French ‌priest, stunned the ​mission world.

sections.label: Shinto Sources
sections.body: The ​island's ‌sanctuaries ‌guard ​the ​two ​shores of ​its ​myth. ‌**Takachiho ​shrine** ​in ‌the ​mountains ‌keeps ​the ‌descent ​of ​Ninigi ​— the ​cavern ​of ‌Amaterasu ​(Ama-no-Iwato) ‌is ​the ‌pilgrimage's ​other ‌anchor, ​where ‌the ​sun returned ​to ‌the ‌world. ‌**Usa ​Jingū**, ​mother-shrine ‌of ​the ​Hachiman ‌cult, ​stands ​on ‌the coast ​that ‌faced ​Korea: ​the ​oracular ​god ‌of ‌warriors ​whose ‌priests ​answered ​the ‌state for ‌a ‌thousand ‌years. ​**Hakata's** ‌shore ​temples ​mark ​the ‌Mongol ​anchorage ​of ​the kamikaze, ‌and ​**Ōura** ​and ​the ‌hidden-Christian ​sites ‌of ​Nagasaki ‌— ​UNESCO-listed ‌— ‌keep ​the century ​of ​the ​forbidden ‌faith ‌in ​stone.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Kyūshū is ​the island that ‌opens. Rice, writing, ‌Buddhism, gunpowder, ​Christianity, Western science ​— all knocked ​on this shore, ​and Japan answered ​differently each ‌time: embrace, storm, ​secrecy, translation. It ​asks the gateway's ‌question, which is ​every border's ‌question: what do ​you let in ‌— and what ​does the letting-in ​make of ​you?

The gateway's ​pattern persists in ​silicon: the island ‌that took in ​rice, iron, ‌scripture, and surgery ​now takes in ‌the semiconductor supply ​chain, and Kumamoto's ‌fabs are ​Tsukushi's old role ‌in new matter. ​Every borderland knows ​its double exposure ‌— first to ‌the gift, ‌first to the ​invasion — and ​Kyūshū's answer has ‌been constant for ​two thousand ​years: translate everything, ‌fear nothing twice, ​and keep the ​door's hinges oiled.

‌And the ​island's two great ‌memories — the ​divine wind and ​the atomic one ​— face ​each other across ‌eight centuries: the ‌storm that saved ​and the bomb ‌that burned, ​both arriving from ​the same sky ‌over the same ‌coast. Kyūshū carries ‌them without resolving ‌them, which ​is the gateway's ‌last lesson: the ​shore that opens ​to the world ​must be ‌ready for everything ​the world brings, ​the sutra and ​the cannonball, the ‌virus and ​the vaccine, the ​answer arriving, as ​always, by sea.

‌The straits have ​not moved; ‌the gateway still ​opens each morning ‌to the same ​west. What changes ‌is only ‌the cargo — ​sutras once, silicon ​now — and ​the island's ancient ​readiness to ‌receive it, translate ‌it, and make ​it Japanese.[^1]
